:::{#thm-consistency}
#### When a linear system has a solution

Let $\matr{A}$ be $m \times n$, let $\vecf{b} \in \reals^m$,
and let $\matr{G}$ be any generalized inverse of $\matr{A}$ (@def-generalized-inverse).
The following statements are equivalent:

1. $\matr{A} \vecf{x} = \vecf{b}$ is consistent (@def-consistent-system);
2. $\vecf{b} \in \mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$ (@def-column-space);
3. $\matr{A} \matr{G} \vecf{b} = \vecf{b}$.

:::

::: proof

**1 and 2 are equivalent.**
Statement 1 says $\vecf{b} = \matr{A} \vecf{x}$ for some $\vecf{x}$ (@def-consistent-system), and
$\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$ is the set of vectors $\matr{A} \vecf{x}$ (@def-column-space),
so $\vecf{b}$ is in it exactly when $\vecf{b} = \matr{A} \vecf{x}$ for some $\vecf{x}$.

**1 implies 3.**
By @thm-generalized-inverse-solves, $\matr{G} \vecf{b}$ is a solution,
so $\matr{A}\,(\matr{G} \vecf{b}) = \vecf{b}$,
which is statement 3 (@thm-matmul-assoc).

**3 implies 1.**
If $\matr{A} \matr{G} \vecf{b} = \vecf{b}$,
then $\vecf{x} = \matr{G} \vecf{b}$ is a solution,
since $\matr{A}\,(\matr{G} \vecf{b}) = (\matr{A} \matr{G})\,\vecf{b}$ (@thm-matmul-assoc).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-consistency}
#### Testing consistency with a generalized inverse

For $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$
and the generalized inverse $\matr{G} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 5 \\ 7 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$,
$\matr{A} \matr{G} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$.

- $\vecf{b} = (2, 0)$:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  \matr{A} \matr{G} \vecf{b} &= (2, 0) \\
  &= \vecf{b},
  \end{aligned}
  $$

  so the system is consistent.
- $\vecf{b} = (2, 1)$: $\matr{A} \matr{G} \vecf{b} = (7, 0) \ne \vecf{b}$, so it is not,
  as @exm-generalized-inverse-solves found directly.

:::
